body.p: This study provides fundamental insights into the mechanisms of visual object categorization in primates by establishing a scalable behavioral framework for assessing category learning and generalization in macaque monkeys. The evidence is compelling, supported by extensive behavioral characterization, rigorous control experiments, and comprehensive comparisons with human behavior and computational models.
Summary:

This study presents a systematic behavioral characterization of object classification abilities in macaque monkeys using a high-throughput touchscreen-based paradigm. The work shows that monkeys can learn and generalize many binary object classification rules and compares their behavior with humans and computational models. A key finding is that monkey behavior is more closely aligned with visual deep neural networks, whereas human behavior is better captured by language-informed models. The study provides a useful benchmark for understanding visually grounded object categorization in nonhuman primates.
Strengths:

The study introduces a scalable and well-controlled behavioral paradigm for testing many object classification rules in macaques. The comparison across monkeys, humans, and computational models is a major strength and makes the work broadly relevant to visual neuroscience, comparative cognition, and computational modeling. The results provide an informative framework for distinguishing categorization based primarily on visual representations from categorization supported by semantic or language-based knowledge.
Weaknesses:

Some aspects of the interpretation would benefit from clarification. In particular, it remains somewhat unclear what stimulus-level factors drive image difficulty, how much training performance reflects general rule learning versus repeated reinforcement of specific images, and whether monkeys and humans apply the same category rules. The link between macaque IT representations and monkey behavior is also suggestive but not yet fully resolved, given the limited and separate neural dataset.
Comments on revised version.
The authors have addressed all of my concerns.
Summary:

The paper tackles a very interesting question and provides a solid and systematic piece of data that may be useful for numerous NeuroAI works in the future. The question is how well can macaque monkeys with a "pretrained" visual system without human knowledge learn to categorize images based on different kinds of (sometimes arbitrary) category definitions. In general, I love the paper a lot, and I think both the data and presentation of it are beautiful.
Strengths:
(1) They developed a scalable method for training and studying this behavior and did exhaustive evaluation of monkeys' behavior and learning process.
(2) Beyond the behavior result, they performed extensive analysis and control experiment to isolate the cue monkeys are using to perform the categorization.
(3) The extensive comparison of behavior with deep neural networks is also super interesting.
(4) The authors performed very careful examination of generalization behavior in monkeys, similar to standard practise in machine learning.
(5) The presentation of the data is very beautiful and deliberately designed, kudos to the efforts!

(6) I really enjoyed the further categorization task based on human knowledge, and the arbitrary rule task, this really push our understanding of the visual categorization and learning capability of monkeys.
(7) The examination of *learning dynamics* in human vs monkey is also quite interesting, i.e. human can "understand the rule" and learn much faster versus monkey learning across a few days.
Comments on revised version
The authors have successfully addressed all my previous concerns and incorporated my suggestions regarding the organization and presentation of the results.

The authors have also provided a thorough set of additional analyses regarding the generalization capabilities of DNN models, making the comparisons between humans, monkeys, and DNNs clearer and more accessible.
I am very pleased with the revised version of the manuscript and would like to congratulate the authors on this beautiful work.
The following is the authors’ response to the original reviews.

disp-quote.p: Summary:

This study presents a systematic behavioral characterization of object classification abilities in macaque monkeys using a high-throughput touchscreen-based paradigm. The work shows that monkeys can learn and generalize many binary object classification rules, and compares their behavior with humans and computational models. A key finding is that monkey behavior is more closely aligned with visual deep neural networks, whereas human behavior is better captured by language-informed models. The study provides a useful benchmark for understanding visually grounded object categorization in nonhuman primates.
Strengths:

The study introduces a scalable and well-controlled behavioral paradigm for testing many object classification rules in macaques. The comparison across monkeys, humans, and computational models is a major strength and makes the work broadly relevant to visual neuroscience, comparative cognition, and computational modeling. The results provide an informative framework for distinguishing categorization based primarily on visual representations from categorization supported by semantic or language-based knowledge.

In particular, it remains somewhat unclear what stimulus-level factors drive image difficulty, how much training performance reflects general rule learning versus repeated reinforcement of specific images, and whether monkeys and humans apply the same category rules. body.p: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive evaluation of our study and the constructive feedback. We have carefully considered all comments and conducted additional analyses to clarify the mechanisms of image difficulty, rule generalization versus reinforcement, and the neural/behavioral links.

disp-quote.p: (R1.1) Stimulus-level difficulty and the role of typicality

The authors may consider taking a closer look at the stimulus-level factors that make some images difficult. In Figure 1E and Figure 1F, some images were consistently more difficult for monkeys, with lower accuracy and longer reaction times. The authors mention that these images tend to be atypical examples, such as a coiled snake or roasted chicken. This is an interesting observation, but it is currently mostly qualitative. It would be useful to relate image-level difficulty to more explicit stimulus properties, such as typicality or other available annotations from databases such as THINGS (Kramer et al., 2023, Science Advances). This analysis could help determine whether monkey errors are driven by systematic properties of the stimuli rather than random behavioral variability. Additionally, a more explicit discussion of how stimulus properties such as typicality contribute to image-level difficulty would strengthen the interpretation.

body.p: Thank you for this very important suggestion. Indeed, our observation that the monkeys made errors for atypical exemplars was only qualitative in the original manuscript (Fig. 1E). To quantitatively evaluate this, we followed the reviewer’s suggestion and developed a typicality metric based on Kramer et al. (2023). While Kramer et al. (2023) computed typicality within basic-level categories to predict image memorability, we calculated typicality relative to the rule of a given task (e.g., whether an image is typical within the animate or inanimate category in the animate vs. inanimate task) based on DNN outputs (using AlexNet as an example; similar patterns with other visual DNNs). Importantly, we found that this typicality had a significant positive correlation with the monkeys’ performance quantified as category sensitivity (except for the tools vs. electronics task, which might suggest that the monkeys developed idiosyncratic solutions for this task, consistent with slower learning rate, Fig. 1H). Thus, as the reviewer predicted, image typicality is an important factor that explains the monkey error patterns. We have added these results as Fig. 6I–K and revised the main text accordingly.

disp-quote.p: (R1.2) Training performance versus generalization performance

In Figure 2B, the authors show that monkeys generalized well to both 'old' and 'new' object categories, which is an important result. However, it looks like performance on the training images is still higher than performance on the generalization images. It would be helpful if the authors could clarify how much of the better performance on training images reflects transferable rule learning versus repeated reinforcement. For example, are the images with the largest training-generalization gap also the atypical or difficult images discussed in Figure 1E and Figure 1F? Do difficult training images become correctly classified after repeated training, whereas similar novel images remain difficult during generalization? This would help clarify the extent to which monkeys learned generalizable rules versus reinforced classifications of particular difficult examples.

body.p: Indeed, the higher performance on training images likely reflects the benefit of repeated reinforcement in the tasks in Fig. 2. Nonetheless, as shown in Figure 2B of our manuscript, monkeys exhibited robust generalization to novel categories that were never presented during training (new categories, compared against old categories; Fig. 2A), establishing the presence of transferable rule learning.

The key question is to what extent performance was driven by the transferable rule versus reinforced associations between specific images and choices. We first compared, for each THINGS object category, performance on the repeatedly presented training images and performance on novel, generalization images from the same categories. We found moderate positive correlations (R > 0.38, p < 0.001 in all three tasks; Supplementary Fig. 8A; each dot is an object category), suggesting that monkeys used transferable rules between the repeated and novel images.

We further used image typicality to address this question. Here, we averaged the typicality of all images within each THINGS object category for a given rule (e.g., the typicality of dog or squirrel images under the ‘animate’ rule) and compared it with the average monkey performance for the same images in that category. The rationale is that, if the monkeys used a transferable rule, their performance would be more likely to be influenced by image typicality under that rule.

We found results consistent with this. In all three THINGS tasks, typicality was correlated with behavioral performance for both new and old category images. The correlations were weaker for the training images, consistent with the idea that repeated reinforcement reduced the influence of image content itself (ceiling performance may also have contributed). We have reported these findings in the revised Supplementary Fig. 8 and revised the text accordingly.

disp-quote.p: (R1.3) Do monkeys and humans apply the same category rule?

The discrepancy between monkey, human, and model performance raises an important conceptual question: when monkeys perform worse than humans or DNNs, are they making errors while applying the same category rule, or are they relying on a somewhat different representational basis? Because monkeys infer the rule through trial and error, the rule they learn may not be identical to the explicit semantic rule used by humans. For example, in a mammal vs. non-mammal task, humans can use prior knowledge to classify atypical cases such as bats, whereas monkeys may rely more on visual similarity to familiar mammals or non-mammals.

One useful analysis would be to identify the object categories or images on which monkeys consistently make errors, and test whether these errors are shared across animals. If the same images or categories are difficult across monkeys, this would suggest systematic constraints in the monkeys' internal category structure rather than random mistakes. It would also be informative to compare these difficult items with human RTs, DNN confidence, and available typicality or semantic measures. This could help distinguish whether the monkey-human gap reflects decision noise or a more qualitative difference in the representational basis of categorization.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this important recommendation. Following your advice, we quantified the similarity of error/performance patterns across subjects. Since we developed a unified metric for stimulus difficulty (category sensitivity (k) in Fig. 6) that works for both human and monkey data, we used this to select difficult images and compare individual subjects’ performance. This sensitivity (k) for each image was defined such that larger positive numbers indicate higher performance. When we compared this across images and tasks between pairs of monkeys (average of the three pairs), we found positive correlations (R = 0.33), indicating that they made errors for similar images, as the reviewer predicted. We also found similar levels of correlations between pairs of human participants (R = 0.30). However, when we compared between individual monkeys and humans, we found positive but lower correlations (R = 0.17; Fig. 6L). Also, as indicated in Fig. 6F, when the sensitivity averaged across subjects was compared between humans and monkeys, we found clear positive correlations (R = 0.30–0.43).

Together, we believe these results suggest two points. First, moderate positive correlations between individual monkeys and between the species indicate that monkeys indeed made shared errors, which were also partially shared with humans. We consider that these error patterns can be partly explained by the typicality of images as shown in Fig. 6L. Second, at the same time, the correlations between individual monkeys and humans were lower, suggesting that the two species followed somewhat different rules. We think this finding naturally connects to our last figure in the manuscript (Fig. 7), in which we showed differences between humans and monkeys in their similarity to vision models.
We have added this subject-level correlation plot as Fig. 6L in the revised manuscript and added a paragraph to explain this. Thank you again for this suggestion.

disp-quote.p: (R1.4) Is macaque IT sufficient to explain monkey categorization behavior?

The neural interpretation of the monkey-visual DNN similarity could also be developed further. In Figure 4, monkey behavior appears to exceed what is predicted from the available IT responses. This raises the possibility that downstream areas may transform IT representations into more abstract or task-relevant decision variables. However, since the neural sample used here is limited and comes from an existing dataset rather than from the same animals performing the same tasks, it is hard to know whether IT is truly insufficient, or whether the apparent gap simply reflects limited sampling.

One possible way to address this would be to use a scaling analysis similar in spirit to Rajalingham et al. (2021), estimating how decoding performance changes as more IT neurons are included. This could provide a better estimate of whether a sufficiently large IT population would be expected to reach the level of monkey behavior, or even exceed it.

The interpretation would be quite different depending on the result. If the estimated IT ceiling remains below monkey behavior, this would suggest that downstream areas may be needed to encode more abstract task rules or decision variables. If the estimated IT ceiling reaches or exceeds monkey behavior, then IT may already contain enough category information, and the behavioral limitations may instead come from readout, learning, or decision processes. An especially interesting possibility is that IT representations might align with human behavior better than monkey behavior does. This would suggest that macaque IT contains category-relevant structure that is qualitatively similar to human category rules, but that monkeys make more errors because they do not read out this structure as efficiently.

body.p: This is a very important question. Indeed, in the original plot, the IT performance tended to be lower than the monkey performance. To check if this is really the case, we followed the reviewer’s recommendation and calculated IT decoding performance as a function of the number of units (Rajalingham et al., 2020). To be compatible with the monkey experiments, we trained a linear classifier using the training set of each task and tested its generalization performance on the test set. Even at the plateau reached with the largest number of units, IT performance remained below the monkeys’ performance in some tasks (Fig. 5D).

We wondered whether IT really does not contain sufficient information to explain monkey performance and took another classification approach: performing 5-fold cross-validated linear classification within the generalization set, which provides more training samples to construct a classifier. This method yielded IT decoding performance comparable to the monkeys’ generalization performance (Panel B).

We therefore conclude that IT cortex contains sufficient information to explain monkey performance, and that the lower performance arose from the constraints on classifier training that we imposed to mimic the monkey experiments. This might imply that monkeys adopt some better learning strategies than we used here or leveraged prior experience to learn the tasks with fewer training samples required to train the IT classifier. We discussed this point in the revised manuscript (revised Fig. 5D, E). Thank you again for this important suggestion.

body.p: We would like to express sincere thanks to the reviewer for the kind endorsement of our manuscript. We have fully addressed your suggestions as below.

I feel there are two topics in the section, one is the stress test of monkey categorization on semantics-related tasks, and the other is the general behavior comparison between humans, monkeys, and a vast set of neural networks. body.p: Thank you for the suggestion. We agree with the suggestion and have split original Figure 6 into Figure 4 and Figure 7 in the revised manuscript.

body.p: Indeed, this conveys somewhat separate messages compared with the preceding or following paragraphs, but given that we have a series of control experiments, and the number of sections is already somewhat large, we decided to keep all these control experiments in one section. Nonetheless, following the reviewer’s suggestion, we moved original Fig. 6AB (now Fig. 4) right after these controls to continue the topic of what categorization rules monkeys could learn and what they could not learn.

disp-quote.p: (R2.6) For Figure 2C, for inanimate categories, the accuracy for natural vs. artificial and animate vs. inanimate accuracy is quite close; but for animate categories, there are a few categories where animate vs. inanimate and mammal vs. non-mammal accuracy are quite different. The authors mentioned the 'fish' category, which kind of fails to generalize. Can authors discuss further what this difference entails, and what does this tell us about the 'conceptual' space of monkeys?

body.p: Thank you for this important question. Indeed, for example, under the animate-inanimate task, the monkeys showed poor performance on “fish” category. As shown in Fig. 1E, the monkeys consistently performed well on some images and poorly on others. These error patterns were shared across monkeys (Fig. 6L in the revised manuscript) and partly consistent with human behavior (Fig. 6F). To further clarify what these error patterns entail, and also following Reviewer 1’s suggestion, we computed the typicality of each image for each given rule (e.g., how typical fish images are among all animate images in the animate-inanimate task) based on the outputs of DNNs. We found that this typicality was significantly correlated with the monkey performances in most tasks (Fig. 6I-K in the revised manuscript; we found the tools-electronics task could not be explained by this, consistent with the monkeys’ lower learning speed for this task as well, Fig. 1H). We therefore suspect that monkey behavior partly depended on whether images were typical exemplars in a category or not. We have added these new analyses in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (R2.7) Figure S3 presented a very interesting sub-investigation. i.e., training the rule on normal animate vs. inanimate fails to generalize on texform animate vs. inanimate, but training on texform animate vs. inanimate seems to show a bit of generalization to the texform held-out set. This is a very cool result, and 'they could not generalize the rule to texform images' in L174 undersells this result and was slightly misleading. So I'd suggest the authors discuss this Figure S3 finding with some more sentences in the main text, and its implications, e.g., distribution shift leading to non-generalization, etc.

body.p: Thank you so much for your suggestion. We fully agree that this texform control is an important one. We therefore moved these panels to one of the main figures and discussed these results using a full paragraph in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (R2.8) (a) Are there some DNN generalization results for Figure 2D and Figure S3 results for these generalization/domain shifts? I feel it will be a very interesting comparison if there is a difference in DNN generalization behaviors.
(b) Similarly, are there DNN generalization results for Figure 3A, B experiments? It will be very interesting too, how DNN can classify these arbitrary boundaries and 'generalize' or not.

body.p: Thank you for this suggestion. Following this recommendation, we have systematically evaluated DNN generalization across all domain-shift conditions (including the Figure 2D control tasks such as silhouette, outline, as well as Texform and Randomization tasks). Overall, the performance of visual DNNs was qualitatively comparable to monkey behavior; they performed reasonably well on our domain-shift images, and performed much worse on the concrete category-level randomization task (Supplementary Figure 6B) that had no common rule (but still images in the same basic-level categories were associated with the same targets, allowing them to perform above chance). They also did not generalize the animate vs. inanimate rule well to the text-form images (panel C left). Thus, we found overall similarity between monkey behavior and visual DNNs. These results are summarized in the revised Supplementary Figure 6 with additional text. Thank you again for this suggestion.

disp-quote.p: (c) For monkey learning curves (Figures 1D, 1H, 3C), could you provide a version with trials as x unit? This facilitates comparison with the human learning curve (Figure 5A). Does that make sense?

body.p: We agree that trial-based learning curves provide a clearer and more direct comparison with human learning dynamics. In the revised manuscript, we have added the learning curves for monkeys with trial count as x-axis (the revised Figure 1H and Supplementary Fig. 3).

disp-quote.p: (d) One thing this paper did a super good job at is to examine the generalization of categorization behavior, which could be emphasized via the title or abstract.

body.p: Thank you for your kind words and this suggestion. We agree that generalization performance is one of the most important results when evaluating monkey behavior. We have emphasized this point in the revised Abstract as follows:

“Here, we developed a task paradigm that enabled us to train monkeys on a large battery of binary classification tasks using natural object images, spanning more than 10 rules, such as animate versus inanimate, natural versus man-made objects, and mammalian versus nonmammalian animals. We then evaluated their performance on novel, generalization stimuli. Monkeys acquired each rule in a few days, generalized it well, and exhibited error patterns consistent with human judgments.”
